intro: Most of what you will read for the rest of your life is not a story. It is a news article, a science page, a letter from a landlord, a speech, a post someone shared, a report your boss hands you. Nonfiction is the reading that runs the world, and it does not always tell you the truth. Two people who stood a block apart during the Great Chicago Fire wrote two different accounts of it. Three captions on one flood photo told three different stories. Learning to read this kind of text well is learning to see what a writer is really saying, what they are leaving out, and whether their evidence holds.

This unit moves in three steps. First, you learn to find the central idea of a nonfiction text, trace how its details build that idea, notice its structure and tone, and compare two writers on the same subject. Second, you take apart arguments: claim, evidence, reasoning, the other side, the fallacies that fool people, and then you build an argument of your own and defend it in a debate with rules. Third, you go to the sources themselves: who made them, why, when, what they show, and how to borrow from them honestly with quotes, paraphrases and citations.

By the end you will be able to read an editorial and say exactly where it holds and where it breaks. You will be able to write an argument that a school board would have to take seriously. And you will have a habit that most adults never build: before you believe or share something, you find out where it came from. That habit is worth more than any single fact in this unit.
bigQuestion: How do you find out what is true, prove it to someone else, and give credit for what you learned?

timeline.t: You read two accounts of one event and find the central idea of each.
You write an objective summary: the idea and key details, no opinions.
You notice how the writer organized the text and what each word's tone does.
You sort sentences into facts, opinions and reasoned judgments.
You pick a claim you can defend and gather evidence with sources.
You write the reasoning that connects each piece of evidence to the claim.
You state the other side fairly and answer it, without a single fallacy.
You debate with timed turns while judges score evidence, not volume.
You check a source sideways: who made it, why, when, and what others say.
You paraphrase, quote and cite, and build a works cited page.
You present your findings on slides that point, while you do the talking.

test.q: Which of these is a central idea rather than a topic?
choices: The Great Chicago Fire spread fast because the city was dry, windy and built of wood
test.why: A central idea is a full sentence that makes a point about the topic.

test.q: Which sentence does NOT belong in an objective summary?
choices: The article explains why water mains break in winter
The writer says old pipes crack when the ground shifts
Honestly, the city should be ashamed
The article names the city's replacement program
test.why: An objective summary keeps the reader's opinion out.

test.q: "Because the summer was dry, the fire spread quickly." Which text structure is this?
test.why: Because signals that one thing made another happen.

test.q: The tailor and the teacher wrote different accounts of the same fire mainly because
choices: their purpose, position and knowledge differed
test.why: Honest witnesses differ based on where they stood, what they knew and why they wrote.

test.q: A speech given by Lincoln in 1863 is best described as
test.why: A speech made at the time by a person involved is a primary source.

test.q: "The city's rebuilding was a triumph." This is
test.why: Triumph is a judging word. The sentence states a belief that cannot be proved.

test.q: Which of these is the strongest claim?
choices: Some people have opinions about school hours
Our middle school should start no earlier than 8:30
test.why: A strong claim is specific, arguable and supportable.

test.q: A writer gives a claim and evidence, but the reader still asks "so what?" What is missing?
test.why: Reasoning explains how the evidence supports the claim. Without it the link is invisible.

test.q: "Everyone knows the early bell is bad, so it must be." This fallacy is
test.why: Bandwagon claims something is true because many people believe it.

test.q: Why does a strong argument include a counterclaim?
choices: Because the rules require exactly five paragraphs
Because a reader who knows the objection will distrust a writer who ignores it
test.why: Naming and answering the other side shows fairness and earns trust.

test.q: In a classroom debate, judges score
choices: the claim, evidence, reasoning and rebuttal
test.why: A rubric scores the quality of the argument, not the judge's own view.

test.q: What was true about the flood photo Rosa checked?
choices: It was real but four years old and from a different street
test.why: The image search showed a real Chicago photo from a water main break four years earlier.

choices: checking what independent sources say about a source
test.why: Reading sideways across other sources tells you more about a source than its own pages can.

test.q: You paraphrase an idea in your own words. Do you cite the source?
choices: No, it is your writing now
Yes, because the idea came from the source
test.why: Credit goes to ideas, not just words.

test.q: An MLA works cited page is ordered
choices: by the order sources were found
by how useful each source was
alphabetically by the author's last name
test.why: Alphabetical order lets readers find any entry from the in-text citation.

write.prompt: Take a stand: Should middle schools start no earlier than 8:30 in the morning? Write an argument with a clear claim, at least three pieces of evidence from this unit's chapters (the doctors' recommendation, the sleep survey, the bus and budget concerns, the students with jobs), reasoning for each, a fairly stated counterclaim with a rebuttal, and in-text citations for anything you borrow.
tips: State your claim in one specific sentence at the end of your introduction.
Use evidence a reader could check, and name where each piece came from.
After every piece of evidence, write the reasoning: this shows, therefore, this means.
State the strongest version of the other side, then answer it with evidence, not volume.
Check your draft for bandwagon, ad hominem and false choice before anyone else does.

title: Nonfiction and Argument

chapters.title: Central Idea and Evidence
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you find what a piece of nonfiction is really saying, and how do you know whether to trust it?

story.title: One Block Apart, Two Different Fires
story.kicker: On the night of October 8, 1871, Chicago began to burn. Two neighbors watched the same flames and wrote two very different accounts.
paragraphs: The Great Chicago Fire started on the evening of Sunday, October 8, 1871, in a barn on DeKoven Street on the city's near southwest side. The summer had been dry, the wind was strong, and most of the city was built of wood. By the time rain finally put the fire out on October 10, about three hundred people were dead, roughly a hundred thousand had lost their homes, and more than three square miles of the city were ash. The old stone Water Tower on Michigan Avenue still stands today, one of the few buildings that survived.

Now picture two neighbors who lived a block apart that night. Their letters are imagined for this chapter, but people like them were real. The first neighbor, a tailor, writes to his brother: "The wind carried burning boards over our heads like leaves. I put my wife and the children in a cart and pushed them north for two hours. Behind us the sky was orange. I did not look back until we reached the river."

The second neighbor, a schoolteacher, writes in her diary: "The fire bells rang for an hour before anyone in our building moved. The firemen were exhausted from a large blaze the night before. If the city had kept more engines on the west side, the fire would have been stopped at the river. This was not bad luck. This was bad planning."

Read the two accounts again. The tailor tells you what he saw and felt. His central idea is something like: the fire was terrifying and we barely escaped. The teacher tells you what she thinks caused the disaster. Her central idea is: the city could have stopped this fire. Same night, same block, two central ideas.

Both accounts are useful. Neither is the whole story. A good reader of nonfiction does what a detective does: finds the main point of each account, checks which details support it, notices the writer's tone and purpose, and then compares the accounts to get closer to what really happened. That is the work of this chapter.
story.think: Which neighbor's account would you trust more if you wanted to know what the fire felt like? Which one if you wanted to know what caused it to spread? Why?

lessons.title: Topic Is Not the Same as Idea
lessons.mainIdea: A topic is what a text is about; the central idea is what the text says about that topic, and it is always a full sentence.
reading: Ask a student what an article is about and you may hear one word: "Sharks." That word is the *topic*. But a text is never just about sharks. It says something about sharks. "Most shark species are harmless to people" is a sentence. That sentence is the *central idea*: the main point the writer wants you to take away. A topic is a word or phrase. A central idea is a whole sentence with a claim in it.

Here is a short paragraph written for this lesson. "Chicago's Water Tower looks like a small castle, but it was built in 1869 to hold a tall standpipe that evened out the pressure of water pumped from Lake Michigan. When the Great Fire burned the neighborhood around it in 1871, its limestone walls did not burn. Today it stands on Michigan Avenue as a reminder of the city that rebuilt itself." The topic is the Water Tower. The central idea is bigger: a plain working building became a symbol of Chicago's survival.

To find the central idea, ask two questions. First: what is this mostly about? That gives you the topic. Second: what does the writer most want me to understand about it? Answer in a full sentence, and you have the central idea. Longer texts can have more than one central idea, one per section, and one bigger idea that ties them together.

Watch out for a common mistake. A single interesting detail is not the central idea. "The Water Tower was built in 1869" is true and specific, but the paragraph is not mostly about that date. The central idea has to cover most of the details in the text, not just one of them.

words.d: what a text is about, said in a word or short phrase
the main point a nonfiction text makes about its topic, stated as a full sentence
a specific fact, example or description that supports a central idea

look.title: Three Sentences, One Central Idea
look.text: A paragraph says: Monarch butterflies fly up to 3,000 miles from Canada to Mexico each fall. No single butterfly makes the whole round trip; it takes several generations. Scientists still do not fully understand how the young butterflies find a place they have never seen.
look.prompt: What is the topic? Now write the central idea as one full sentence that covers all three details.

check.q: Which of these is a central idea, not just a topic?
choices: The Water Tower became a symbol of a city that rebuilt itself
check.why: A central idea is a full sentence that says something about the topic. The other choices are only topics or details.

check.q: Why is "The Water Tower was built in 1869" not the central idea of the model paragraph?
choices: It is one detail, and the central idea has to cover most of the details
It has a number in it
check.why: One detail, even a true one, is not the main point. The central idea covers most of what the text says.

check.q: What is the second question you ask to find a central idea?
choices: What does the writer most want me to understand about the topic?
check.why: The first question finds the topic. The second finds what the writer says about that topic, which is the central idea.

lessons.title: How Details Build an Idea
lessons.mainIdea: Writers develop a central idea with details such as facts, examples, numbers and quotations, and each detail should push the idea forward.
reading: A central idea with no details is just a claim floating in the air. "Lake Michigan is dangerous for swimmers." Says who? Now add details. "Rip currents form along Chicago's beaches when waves pile water against the shore. In some summers, more people drown in Lake Michigan than in any other Great Lake. Lifeguards fly red flags on days when the current is strong." Now the idea has legs to stand on.

Nonfiction writers use a small set of detail types again and again. Facts: things that can be checked. Numbers and statistics: counts and measurements. Examples: one specific case that shows the idea. Quotations: the words of a person who knows. Descriptions: what something looks or sounds like. When you read, label the details. It helps you see how the writer is building.

Good writers do not pile up details at random. Each one *develops* the idea, meaning it adds a new piece. In the lake paragraph, the first detail explains how the danger happens, the second shows how serious it is, and the third shows what people do about it. Take one detail away and the idea gets weaker. That is the test of a detail that belongs.

Try this when you read a paragraph: draw a line, put the central idea at the top, and hang each detail under it. If a detail does not hang from the idea, either the writer wandered or you have the wrong central idea. Both are worth noticing.

words.d: to build an idea up by adding details that make it fuller and clearer
a number that comes from counting or measuring something
the exact words someone said or wrote, set inside quotation marks

look.title: Details in a Model Paragraph
look.cite: A seven-sentence paragraph on rip currents, written and counted for this lesson
look.prompt: This writer used mostly facts and numbers. What kind of central idea might need more quotations or examples instead?

check.q: What does a detail do for a central idea?
choices: It supports and builds the idea
It makes the text longer for no reason
check.why: Details develop the central idea by giving it facts, examples and other support.

check.q: Which of these is a statistic?
choices: The lake was gray and cold
Rip currents form when waves push water against the shore
check.why: A statistic is a number from counting or measuring. Twelve people is a count.

check.q: You find a detail that does not connect to the central idea you wrote down. What might that mean?
choices: You may have the wrong central idea, or the writer wandered
The text has no central idea
You should skip the rest of the text
check.why: Every detail should hang from the central idea. A loose detail is a sign to check your idea or the writer's focus.

lessons.title: The Objective Summary
lessons.mainIdea: An objective summary restates a text's central idea and key details in your own words, without adding your opinion.
reading: Your friend missed the article and asks what it said. You could read it aloud, but that would take ten minutes. Instead you say: "It's about rip currents in Lake Michigan. They form when waves push water against the beach, they cause more drownings than people expect, and lifeguards use flags to warn swimmers." That is a *summary*: the central idea plus the key details, shorter, in your own words.

Now notice what you did not say. You did not say "and I think swimming there is stupid." That is your opinion, and it does not belong in an *objective* summary. Objective means you keep yourself out of it. You report what the writer said, not what you think about it. A test: if the writer read your summary, they should nod and say "yes, that is what I wrote."

Here is a way to build one. Start with the central idea in one sentence. Add the two or three details that matter most, in the order the writer used. Leave out small examples, jokes and repeated points. Use your own words, except for a key term you cannot replace. Keep it to about a quarter of the original length, or less.

A summary is not a list of everything, and it is not a review. "This article was boring" is a review. "The article explains how rip currents form and how to stay safe" is a summary. Learning the difference will help you in every class where a teacher says "tell me what you read."

words.d: a short restatement of a text's central idea and most important details
based on the facts of the text, with no personal opinion added

look.title: Which One Is Objective?
look.text: Two students summarize the same article about the Chicago Water Tower. Ana: "The article says the Water Tower was built in 1869 to hold a standpipe, survived the 1871 fire, and became a symbol of the city." Deshawn: "The article says the Water Tower is the coolest building in Chicago and everyone should visit it."
look.prompt: Which summary is objective? What did the other student add that the writer probably never said?

check.q: Which sentence belongs in an objective summary?
choices: I think the writer is wrong about the lake
This was the best article I read all year
Rip currents form when waves push water against the shore
Everyone should be scared of the lake
check.why: An objective summary restates what the text says. The other choices are opinions or reviews.

check.q: About how long should a summary be compared with the original?
check.why: A summary is much shorter than the text, usually a quarter of the length or less.

check.q: Why should you use your own words in a summary?
choices: Because the writer's words are always wrong
Because copying sentences shows you did not understand the idea
Because your teacher cannot read the original
check.why: Restating in your own words proves you understood the idea, not just copied it.

lessons.title: Four Ways to Organize
lessons.mainIdea: Nonfiction writers organize text in patterns such as time order, cause and effect, compare and contrast, and problem and solution, and signal words reveal the pattern.
reading: Read this: "First the barn caught fire. Then the wind carried sparks to the next block. By midnight the fire had jumped the river." The writer is telling events in the order they happened. That pattern is *chronological* order, or time order. Signal words like first, then, next, by midnight and finally give it away.

Now read this: "Because the summer had been dry and the buildings were wood, the fire spread fast. As a result, the fire department could not keep up." This is *cause and effect*: one thing makes another thing happen. Signal words: because, so, as a result, therefore, led to. A writer uses this pattern to explain why something happened.

Two more patterns are common. *Compare and contrast* shows how two things are alike and different: "Both letters describe the fire, but the tailor focuses on fear while the teacher focuses on blame." Signal words: both, similarly, however, on the other hand, unlike. *Problem and solution* names a difficulty and then how it was fixed: "After the fire, Chicago faced a housing crisis. The city answered with new building codes and brick construction." Signal words: problem, solution, answer, solved.

Most long texts mix patterns. An article might tell a story in time order, pause to explain a cause, then compare two responses. Your job is to notice the pattern in each part. Once you see the shape, the details fall into place and the text is much easier to remember.

words.d: arranged in the order that events happened in time
a pattern that shows how one thing makes another thing happen
a pattern that shows how two things are alike and different
a word or phrase, such as because or however, that shows how ideas connect

look.title: Name the Pattern
look.text: Paragraph A: Unlike the North Side, which was rebuilt in brick within a few years, parts of the West Side kept wooden houses for decades. Paragraph B: The city lacked clean water after the fire, so engineers built a new pumping station beside the Water Tower.
look.prompt: Which pattern does each paragraph use? Which signal words told you?

check.q: Which words signal cause and effect?
check.why: Because, as a result and therefore show that one thing made another happen.

check.q: "The tailor focused on fear while the teacher focused on blame." What pattern is this?
check.why: The sentence shows how two accounts differ. That is compare and contrast.

check.q: Why do writers use chronological order?
choices: To show how two things are alike
To offer a fix for a difficulty
To tell events in the order they happened
check.why: Chronological order follows time. It is the pattern for telling what happened step by step.

lessons.title: Why This Order?
lessons.mainIdea: Analyzing structure means asking why a writer put a paragraph or section where it is, and what the text would lose if it moved.
reading: Knowing the pattern is step one. Step two is asking why. A writer chooses where every paragraph goes. An article about the fire could start with the death toll, or with a single family in a cart, or with the dry summer that set the stage. Each choice does a different job. Starting with the family pulls you in. Starting with the death toll shocks you. Starting with the weather prepares you to understand the cause.

Here is a model text written for this lesson. Its first paragraph describes a girl on a Chicago beach watching a red flag go up. Its second paragraph explains what a rip current is. Its third gives a drowning statistic. Its fourth tells swimmers what to do. Ask: why put the girl first? Because a reader cares about a person before a fact. Why put the statistic third and not first? Because after you understand the current, the number means more.

Now try moving a piece. Put the statistic first. The article becomes colder and more alarming. Put the advice first. Now the reader gets instructions before knowing why they matter. Neither is wrong, but each changes the reading. Noticing this is what teachers mean by *analyzing structure*: seeing that the order is a choice and explaining what the choice does.

When you write about structure, use sentences like these. "The writer opens with a story to make the reader care." "The writer saves the statistic until after the explanation so the number has meaning." "The final section gives advice, which turns fear into action." Every sentence names a part, its place, and its effect.

words.d: the way a text's parts are arranged and how they fit together
to break something into its parts and explain how the parts work

look.title: Move the Paragraph
look.text: An article about school lunches has four paragraphs: 1. A student describes a soggy tray. 2. The cost of a lunch and what the district gets from the state. 3. A comparison with a district that cooks fresh food. 4. Three changes the school board could vote on.
look.prompt: What would change for the reader if paragraph 4 came first? Why do you think the writer put the soggy tray first?

check.q: What does it mean to analyze a text's structure?
choices: To explain why the parts are arranged as they are and what that does
To rewrite the text in your own words
check.why: Analyzing structure means seeing the order as a choice and explaining its effect on the reader.

check.q: In the model text, why does the writer put the girl on the beach first?
choices: Because the writer forgot the statistic
Because a reader cares about a person before a fact
Because it is the shortest paragraph
check.why: Opening with a person draws the reader in. The facts come after the reader cares.

check.q: If the drowning statistic moved to the first paragraph, what would probably happen?
choices: The number would mean less to the reader
The article would be more alarming from the start
check.why: Starting with a shocking number changes the mood. The reading gets colder and more alarming right away.

lessons.title: Word Choice and Tone
lessons.mainIdea: Tone is the writer's attitude toward the subject, and you hear it in the exact words the writer chose.
reading: Read two sentences about the same event. "The fire department responded to the blaze." "The fire department crawled toward the blaze." Both say the firefighters went. But crawled tells you the writer thinks they were slow, maybe even blames them. Responded is neutral. One word changes the whole feeling. That feeling, the writer's attitude toward the subject, is the *tone*.

Tone shows up in nouns and verbs, not just adjectives. "The crowd gathered" is calm. "The mob swarmed" is frightened or scornful. "The mayor stated" is neutral. "The mayor insisted" hints that someone doubted him. "The mayor whined" is openly mocking. When you notice a word that could have been plainer, ask what the writer gained by choosing it.

Words also carry *connotation*, the feeling attached to a word beyond its plain meaning. Thrifty and cheap both mean careful with money, but thrifty sounds like praise and cheap sounds like an insult. Nonfiction writers who want to seem fair choose words with little connotation. Writers who want to persuade often reach for words with a lot of it. You can tell one from the other by listening.

Some tone words to keep handy: neutral, formal, serious, urgent, admiring, critical, sarcastic, playful, angry, hopeful. When a teacher asks about tone, pick one of these, then point to the two or three words in the text that create it. Tone is never a guess; it is evidence.

words.d: the writer's attitude toward the subject, shown through word choice
the feeling or idea a word carries beyond its plain dictionary meaning
showing no strong feeling for or against something

look.title: Two Accounts of One Storm
look.text: Version A: The storm passed through the county on Tuesday, taking down about forty trees and leaving some homes without power until morning. Version B: The storm tore through the county on Tuesday, ripping down forty trees and plunging helpless families into darkness for the whole night.
look.cite: Two versions of one report, written for this lesson
look.prompt: List the words that differ between A and B. What tone does each version have, and which would you trust more for the facts?

check.q: What is tone in nonfiction?
choices: The writer's attitude toward the subject
The date the text was written
check.why: Tone is the writer's attitude, and readers hear it in word choice.

check.q: "The mayor whined about the budget." What does the verb whined tell you?
choices: The writer is neutral about the mayor
The writer is mocking the mayor
The writer is quoting the mayor
check.why: Whined has a scornful connotation. It shows the writer looks down on the mayor's complaint.

check.q: A writer who wants to seem fair and factual will usually choose words that are
check.why: Neutral words let the facts speak. Loaded words show the writer is pushing a feeling.

lessons.title: Two Authors, One Topic
lessons.mainIdea: When two authors write about the same topic, compare what each includes, leaves out, and emphasizes, and you will understand the topic better than either author alone.
reading: Go back to the two neighbors. The tailor and the teacher stood a block apart and watched the same fire. One wrote about the terror of escape. The other wrote about the city's failures. Neither lied. Each chose what to include, what to leave out, and what to *emphasize*, meaning what to give the most space and the strongest words. Reading both gives you more than reading either one.

To compare two authors, make three columns. Column one: what does each author include that the other does not? The tailor mentions the cart and the children; the teacher mentions the fire bells and the tired firemen. Column two: what does each emphasize? The tailor emphasizes feelings; the teacher emphasizes causes. Column three: where do they agree? Both say the wind was fierce and the fire moved fast. Agreement between two separate witnesses is strong evidence.

Then ask why the accounts differ. Purpose matters: the tailor is writing to reassure a brother; the teacher is writing to work out her own anger. Position matters: someone fleeing sees different things than someone who stayed. Knowledge matters: the teacher may have read the newspaper and the tailor may not have. None of these make an author wrong, but they explain the shape of what each wrote.

In writing, a comparison sounds like this: "Both accounts describe a fast-moving fire, but the tailor's letter focuses on his family's escape while the teacher's diary blames the city's lack of preparation. Because the teacher had time to reflect, her account offers a cause; because the tailor was fleeing, his offers a scene." Name both, show the difference, explain the reason.

words.d: to give something extra attention or importance
a description of an event by someone who saw it or studied it
the position and experience from which a person sees something

look.title: Two Reports on One Game
look.text: Report A, from a home-team writer: "The Wolves fought hard but fell 3 to 2 after a questionable call in the final minute." Report B, from a visiting-team writer: "The Hawks earned a 3 to 2 win with a late goal that the Wolves' coach argued about for ten minutes."
look.prompt: What do both reports agree on? What does each one emphasize, and why might that be?

check.q: When two honest witnesses agree on a detail, that detail is
check.why: Two separate people reporting the same thing makes it more likely to be true.

check.q: What does it mean to emphasize something in a text?
choices: To put it in quotation marks
To give it extra attention and importance
check.why: Emphasizing means giving something more space or stronger words so the reader notices it.

check.q: Why did the teacher's account offer a cause while the tailor's offered a scene?
choices: The teacher had time to reflect and the tailor was fleeing
The tailor did not know how to write
The teacher was not really there
check.why: Position and purpose shape what a writer includes. Someone reflecting later can think about causes; someone escaping records what they saw.

lessons.title: Letters, Speeches and Diaries
lessons.mainIdea: A primary source is a text made by someone who was there, and it is powerful evidence as long as you remember who wrote it, for whom, and why.
reading: A history textbook about the Civil War was written a hundred and fifty years after it. A soldier's letter home was written the night after a battle. The letter is a *primary source*: a text created by someone who was there at the time. The textbook is a *secondary source*: a text that explains or interprets primary sources. Both are useful, but they are different kinds of evidence.

Primary sources come in many forms. Letters, diaries, speeches, photographs, newspaper reports from the day, laws, maps, and interviews with people who lived through an event. Each one was made for a reason. A letter was written to one person, so it may be honest but also private and one-sided. A speech was written for a crowd, so it is shaped to move that crowd. A diary was written for the writer alone, so it may say what no one else heard.

Read a primary source with three questions. Who made this? What did they want? Who was supposed to read or hear it? Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, given in November 1863, was a speech at the dedication of a cemetery for soldiers killed months earlier. Knowing that tells you why it is short, serious and full of words like dedicate, consecrate and devotion. The occasion shaped the words.

A primary source is not automatically true. A person who was there may have seen only a corner of the event, may have wanted to look good, or may simply have misremembered. Use the same skills you use on any text: find the central idea, check the details, notice the tone, and compare it with another account.

words.d: a text or object made by someone who was there when an event happened
a text that explains or interprets events using primary sources
the event or situation that a speech or piece of writing was made for

look.title: The First Sentence of a Famous Speech
look.text: Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
look.prompt: A score is twenty years. What year is Lincoln pointing back to, and why would he begin a cemetery speech in 1863 by counting back to that year?

check.q: Which of these is a primary source about the Chicago Fire?
choices: A website built in 2020 that explains the fire
A diary written by a Chicagoan in October 1871
check.why: A diary written at the time by someone who was there is a primary source. The others interpret events later.

check.q: Why might a speech and a diary about the same event sound different?
choices: Because speeches are never about real events
Because a speech is shaped for a crowd and a diary is written for the writer alone
check.why: Audience shapes the writing. A speech aims to move listeners; a diary can say private thoughts.

check.q: A primary source should be read
choices: as always true, because the writer was there
with the same care as any text, checking who wrote it and why
check.why: Being there does not make a writer correct or complete. Check the source like any other text.

lessons.title: Graphs and Pictures With the Words
lessons.mainIdea: Graphs, maps and photos carry information the words do not, and reading them well means checking labels, scale and what was left out.
reading: An article about the Chicago Fire shows a map with a dark shape stretching from DeKoven Street north across the river. The words say the fire burned more than three square miles. The map shows you what three square miles looks like against the city's grid. That is what a *visual* is for: it says something faster or clearer than the words alone.

Read a graph like a text. Start with the title: what is being measured? Then the labels on the two sides, called axes: what do the numbers stand for, and in what units? Then the scale: does the bottom of the graph start at zero, or is it cut off to make a small change look huge? A bar that looks twice as tall as another may only be a little taller if the scale starts at 90 instead of 0.

Photographs and drawings need the same care. A photo of a burned block after the fire is real evidence, but it shows one block, not the whole city. A caption tells you what the picture maker wants you to see. Ask what is outside the frame. Ask when the picture was taken. A photo of the Water Tower standing alone in the ash tells a story of survival, but the photographer chose that angle.

Finally, connect the visual back to the text. Does the graph support the writer's central idea, or does it quietly show something the writer did not mention? Sometimes the most interesting fact in an article is in a chart the writer barely discussed. A careful reader reads all of it.

words.d: a picture, map, graph or chart that presents information
one of the two labeled lines on a graph that show what is measured
the range of numbers on a graph and the size of the steps between them
the words printed under a picture that explain it

look.title: Two Boxes on the Same Page
look.cite: A one-page article about city budgets, written and counted for this lesson
look.prompt: More than half the numbers on the page are in the chart. What might a reader miss by skipping it?

check.q: What should you check first when reading a graph?
choices: The title and the axis labels, to learn what is measured
Whether it has a photo next to it
check.why: The title and axis labels tell you what the graph measures and in what units. Everything else depends on that.

check.q: A bar graph starts its scale at 90 instead of 0. What can this do?
choices: Make a small difference look huge
check.why: A cut-off scale stretches small differences. Bars can look very different when the real gap is small.

check.q: Why should you ask what is outside the frame of a photograph?
choices: Because the photographer chose what to show, and the rest is missing
Because photos are always older than the text
check.why: A photo shows one angle at one moment. What was left out may change the story.

lessons.title: Fact or Opinion?
lessons.mainIdea: A fact can be checked and shown true or false; an opinion expresses a belief or feeling that cannot be proved, though it can be argued.
reading: "The Chicago Fire started on October 8, 1871." "The Chicago Fire was the worst thing that ever happened to the city." The first sentence is a *fact*. You can check it against records, and it is either true or false. The second is an *opinion*. It states a belief. You could argue for it or against it, but you could never prove it the way you prove a date.

Facts are not always true. "The fire started on October 12" is a fact statement that happens to be false. Fact does not mean true; it means checkable. That matters, because writers sometimes state false things in a confident, factual voice. Your job is not to trust the tone. Your job is to ask: could this be checked, and has it been?

Opinions often come with signal words: I think, I believe, the best, the worst, should, terrible, wonderful. But not always. "Chicago's rebuilding was a triumph" has no I think in it, and it is still an opinion. Look for words that judge, not just words that announce a belief. Words that judge are the fingerprints of opinion.

One more trap. A sentence can mix the two. "The fire, which killed about three hundred people, proved that wooden cities are foolish." The death toll is a fact. Foolish is an opinion. Good readers pull the two apart, accept the fact if it checks out, and weigh the opinion on its own.

words.d: a statement that can be checked and shown to be true or false
a statement of belief or feeling that cannot be proved, though it can be argued

look.title: Sort the Sentences
look.text: 1. Lake Michigan is one of the five Great Lakes. 2. Lake Michigan is the most beautiful of the Great Lakes. 3. Lake Michigan is 307 miles long. 4. Everyone should visit Lake Michigan at least once. 5. Lake Michigan touches four states.
look.prompt: Which sentences are facts and which are opinions? Which fact statements would you want to check, and how?

check.q: What makes a statement a fact?
choices: It can be checked and shown true or false
check.why: A fact is checkable. It may turn out true or false, but it can be tested against evidence.

check.q: "Chicago's rebuilding was a triumph." Why is this an opinion even without the words I think?
choices: Because triumph is a judging word that cannot be proved
Because it uses the past tense
check.why: Words that judge, like triumph, mark an opinion. Signal words like I think are not required.

check.q: A confident writer states something false as a fact. What should a careful reader do?
choices: Assume all of the text is false
Ask whether the statement can be checked and check it
check.why: Tone proves nothing. Fact statements are tested by checking them, not by how sure the writer sounds.

lessons.title: Reasoned Judgment
lessons.mainIdea: A reasoned judgment is a conclusion built from facts and clear reasoning, stronger than a plain opinion but still open to argument.
reading: Between fact and opinion there is a third kind of statement. "Chicago's fire spread so fast mainly because of dry weather, wind and wooden buildings." That is not a checkable fact in the way a date is. But it is not just a feeling either. It is a conclusion drawn from evidence: weather records, wind reports, building materials. Call it a *reasoned judgment*.

A reasoned judgment has two parts you can inspect: the facts it rests on, and the reasoning that connects them to the conclusion. "The teacher blamed the city; therefore the city was at fault" is weak, because one angry witness is thin evidence. "Fire records show most engines were on the east side, and the fire started on the west; therefore the city's placement of engines slowed the response" is stronger. The facts are more solid and the link is clearer.

When you read a judgment, ask three questions. What facts does the writer offer? Are those facts enough to support the conclusion, or is the writer stretching? Is there another conclusion the same facts could support? A judgment that survives all three questions deserves your respect even if you still disagree.

In your own writing, make your judgments reasoned. Do not write "the city was terrible at fighting fires." Write "the city's fire department, with only about seventeen steam engines for a city of some three hundred thousand people, was too small for a wooden city in a dry season." Now a reader can see your facts and follow your reasoning, which is exactly what you want them to do.

words.d: a conclusion supported by facts and clear reasoning, which can still be debated
a decision or belief reached after thinking about evidence
the thinking that connects facts to a conclusion

look.title: One Fact, One Opinion, One Judgment
look.text: The library was open 42 hours a week last year and 30 hours this year. The library is the best place in the neighborhood. Because the library cut twelve hours and the after-school program moved elsewhere, fewer students now have a quiet place to do homework.
look.cite: Three sentences written for this lesson
look.prompt: Label each sentence: fact, opinion or reasoned judgment. For the judgment, name the facts it rests on and the reasoning that links them.

check.q: What makes a reasoned judgment different from a plain opinion?
choices: It is supported by facts and reasoning you can inspect
It uses the words I think
check.why: A reasoned judgment shows its facts and its reasoning. A plain opinion offers only a belief.

check.q: "One witness blamed the city, so the city was at fault." Why is this weak?
choices: Because one witness is thin evidence for a big conclusion
Because the city can never be at fault
check.why: One person's blame is not enough evidence to support a conclusion about the whole city.

check.q: Which question helps you test a writer's judgment?
choices: How many pages is the text?
Could the same facts support a different conclusion?
Does the writer use long words?
check.why: If the facts could point elsewhere, the judgment is weaker. This is one of the three test questions.

review.q: What is the difference between a topic and a central idea?
choices: A topic is a full sentence; a central idea is one word
A topic is what a text is about; a central idea is what the text says about it
A central idea is always a number
review.why: The topic is a word or phrase. The central idea is a full sentence that makes a point about it.

review.q: Which sentence would NOT belong in an objective summary?
choices: The article explains how rip currents form
The writer describes the flags lifeguards use
The article was way too long and boring
The writer gives a drowning statistic
review.why: An objective summary leaves out the reader's opinions and reviews.

review.q: Which pattern uses the signal words both, however and unlike?
review.why: Those signal words show how two things are alike and different.

review.q: "The firefighters crawled toward the blaze." What does the word crawled reveal?
choices: That the firefighters were on their knees
review.why: Crawled suggests slowness and blame. It shows the writer's attitude, which is tone.

review.q: Why did the tailor and the teacher write such different accounts of the same fire?
choices: Their purpose, position and knowledge shaped what each included
review.why: Honest witnesses differ because of where they stood, what they knew and why they wrote.

review.q: A soldier's letter written the night after a battle is
review.why: A letter written at the time by someone who was there is a primary source.

review.q: What can a graph with a scale that starts at 90 instead of 0 do to a reader?
choices: Make the graph easier to read honestly
review.why: A cut-off scale stretches small gaps so bars look far more different than they are.

review.q: "The fire department, with about seventeen engines for some three hundred thousand people, was too small for a wooden city." This is best called
review.why: The sentence gives facts and connects them to a conclusion, which is a reasoned judgment.

chapters.title: Argument: Claims, Evidence, Reasoning
chapters.bigQuestion: What separates an argument that convinces a careful reader from one that only sounds convincing?

story.title: Three Students, One Bell
story.kicker: Should the school day start later? Three seventh graders stand up to argue. Only two of them brought anything to back it up.
paragraphs: Ms. Okafor's seventh-grade class in Chicago is holding its first debate. The question on the board: Should our school day start at 9:00 instead of 8:00? Three students volunteer to speak. Each gets two minutes. The rest of the class will vote, but not on who they like. They will vote on who made the best argument.

Jalen goes first. "School should start later because everyone is tired. Nobody wants to be here at eight. Ask anybody. It's just obvious, and anyone who disagrees has never been a kid." He sits down to some laughter. A few people clap. Ms. Okafor writes one word on the board: evidence? Under Jalen's name, the space stays empty.

Priya goes second. "School should start later, and here is why. In 2014 the American Academy of Pediatrics, a group of children's doctors, recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 in the morning. They said teenagers' bodies fall asleep later at night, so an early start cuts into the sleep they need. In our own class survey last week, twenty-one of twenty-six students said they get less than eight hours of sleep on school nights. Doctors say we need eight to ten. A later bell would close that gap." Under Priya's name, Ms. Okafor writes: doctors' recommendation, sleep science, class survey.

Marcus goes last, and he argues the other side. "A later start sounds good, but think about what it costs. Our buses also carry elementary students. If we start at nine, the buses run late for them or the district buys more buses, and last year's budget shows there is no money for that. Also, a later start means a later end, and 140 students in this school have after-school jobs or watch younger siblings. Priya is right that sleep matters. But the fix is to end screen time earlier, not to move the bell." Under Marcus's name: bus schedule, budget, student count, response to Priya.

The class votes. Jalen gets three votes. Priya and Marcus split the rest almost evenly. Jalen is surprised. "But everyone agreed with me," he says. Ms. Okafor nods. "They agreed with your claim. You never gave them a reason to. Priya and Marcus gave them evidence and explained why it mattered. That is the difference between an opinion and an argument."
story.think: Priya and Marcus disagreed, yet both got many votes. What did they do that Jalen did not? Could Jalen have made the same claim well?

sections.title: The Three Parts of an Argument

lessons.title: A Claim You Can Defend
lessons.mainIdea: A claim is a debatable statement that an argument sets out to prove, and a strong claim is clear, specific and possible to disagree with.
reading: "Our school should start at 9:00." Someone could argue against that sentence. That is what makes it a *claim*: a statement you take a stand on and are prepared to defend. "Our school starts at 8:00" is not a claim; it is a fact you could check on the website. "Sleep is important" is barely a claim, because almost nobody would argue with it. A real claim has a real other side.

A strong claim is specific. "Schools should change" is too vague to defend. Change how? "Middle schools should start no earlier than 8:30" tells a reader exactly what you want. It is also arguable: a bus director, a parent, or a student with a morning job could disagree. And it can be supported: there are doctors' reports and surveys you could point to. Specific, arguable, supportable. Test every claim against those three words.

A claim usually comes early in an argument, often at the end of the first paragraph in an essay. Some writers call it the thesis. It is one sentence, or two at most. Everything after it works for it. If a paragraph does not help prove the claim, it does not belong in the argument.

Watch for claims that hide. "Many people feel that the school day is too early" is not a claim, because the writer never takes a side. Ask yourself: what do I believe, and what would I want a reader to do or think? Then say it plainly. Readers trust a writer who is willing to be disagreed with.

words.d: a debatable statement that an argument tries to prove
a claim supported by evidence and reasoning, meant to convince a reader
exact and detailed, not vague

look.title: Which Ones Are Claims?
look.text: 1. Our cafeteria serves pizza on Fridays. 2. Our cafeteria should offer a vegetarian option every day. 3. Some students would like better lunches. 4. Homework should be limited to one hour a night in seventh grade. 5. Homework exists.
look.prompt: Which sentences are real claims: specific, arguable and supportable? What is wrong with each of the others?

check.q: What makes a statement a claim?
choices: It is a fact anyone can check
It is debatable and the writer sets out to prove it
It has the word should in it
It is the last sentence of an essay
check.why: A claim is a statement someone could disagree with, which the writer then defends.

check.q: Why is "Schools should change" a weak claim?
choices: Because nobody could agree with it
Because it is too vague to defend
check.why: A strong claim says exactly what should happen. Vague claims cannot be supported or argued.

check.q: "Many people feel the school day is too early." Why is this not a claim?
choices: The writer never takes a side
check.why: A claim states what the writer believes. Reporting what others feel avoids taking a stand.

lessons.title: Evidence Is What You Can Point To
lessons.mainIdea: Evidence is the facts, data, examples and expert statements that support a claim, and it must come from somewhere a reader could check.
reading: Jalen said "everyone is tired." Priya said "twenty-one of twenty-six students in our class survey get less than eight hours of sleep." Both are about tired students. Only one is *evidence*. Evidence is something a reader could check or count: a fact, a number, a specific example, the words of an expert. "Everyone is tired" cannot be checked. Twenty-one of twenty-six can.

Evidence comes in a few main kinds. Facts and statistics: the school starts at 8:00; 140 students have after-school jobs. Expert statements: a doctors' group recommends a later start. Examples: a named district that changed its start time and what happened. Personal experience: what you saw yourself, useful but weak on its own because it is only one person. The strongest arguments mix kinds.

Every piece of evidence needs a source, the place it came from. "Doctors say" is thin. "The American Academy of Pediatrics said in 2014" is solid, because a reader can look it up. In a class survey, say who was asked and when. If you cannot say where evidence came from, treat it as a rumor, not evidence, until you find out.

Here is a paragraph written for this lesson. "A later start would help students learn. When one suburban district moved its high school start from 7:30 to 8:30, the school reported that fewer students were tardy and that first-period grades rose. Our own school's attendance office says first period has the most absences of any period." Two pieces of evidence, each with a source, each pointing at the claim.

words.d: facts, data, examples or expert statements that support a claim
the person, document or place that a piece of evidence came from
a person with deep knowledge of a subject, whose statements carry weight

look.title: Hours of Sleep on a School Night
look.cite: A survey of 26 students in one classroom, written for this lesson
look.prompt: How many students got less than eight hours? Is one classroom enough evidence for a claim about the whole school? What else would you want?

check.q: Which of these is evidence rather than a bare opinion?
choices: It is obvious that kids are tired
In our survey, 21 of 26 students got less than eight hours of sleep
Anyone who disagrees has never been a kid
check.why: Evidence can be checked or counted. A survey number is evidence; the other choices are opinions.

check.q: Why is personal experience weak as evidence when used alone?
choices: Because it is only one person's view
Because it cannot be written down
Because teachers do not allow it
check.why: One person's experience is real but limited. Stronger arguments add facts, data and expert statements.

check.q: What should you do with evidence when you cannot say where it came from?
choices: Use it anyway if it sounds good
Put it first in the essay
Treat it as a rumor until you find the source
check.why: Evidence needs a source a reader could check. Without one, it is not yet evidence.

lessons.title: Reasoning Connects the Two
lessons.mainIdea: Reasoning is the explanation of why a piece of evidence supports the claim, and without it, evidence just sits there.
reading: Read this: "Our school should start later. Twenty-one of twenty-six students get less than eight hours of sleep." Something is missing. The claim is there. The evidence is there. But the writer never says how the number proves the claim. A reader might think: so what? Maybe those students should go to bed earlier. The missing piece is *reasoning*.

Reasoning is the sentence or two that connects evidence to claim. Priya supplied it: "Doctors say teenagers' bodies fall asleep later at night, so an early start cuts into the sleep they need." Now the survey number means something. Students are short on sleep, teens cannot simply fall asleep earlier, therefore a later bell is the fix. Claim, evidence, reasoning. All three, or the argument has a hole.

Reasoning often begins with words like this shows, this means, because, therefore, so. "First period has the most absences. This shows that many students are not getting to school on time, which suggests that the early start is a barrier for them." Notice the writer does not just repeat the evidence. The writer explains what it proves.

When you check your own argument, cover the reasoning with your hand and read only claim and evidence. If a stranger could say "so what?" you need more reasoning. Then read the reasoning alone. Does it actually follow from the evidence, or does it jump to what you wanted to say anyway? Honest reasoning is the hardest and most valuable part.

words.d: the explanation of how evidence supports a claim
a signal word meaning for that reason; it introduces a conclusion

look.title: Claim, Evidence, Reasoning in Three Sentences
look.text: Our school should add a second lunch period. Right now 640 students share one thirty-minute lunch, and the line takes an average of twelve minutes according to last month's student council timing. When a third of the lunch period is spent standing in line, students eat quickly, waste food and return to class hungry, which hurts afternoon learning.
look.cite: A model paragraph written for this lesson
look.prompt: Find the claim, the evidence and the reasoning. Which sentence would leave the biggest hole if it were cut?

check.q: What does reasoning do in an argument?
choices: It explains how the evidence supports the claim
check.why: Reasoning is the bridge from evidence to claim. It tells the reader why the evidence matters.

check.q: A reader looks at your claim and evidence and says "so what?" What is missing?
check.why: "So what?" means the reader cannot see the connection. Reasoning supplies it.

check.q: Which signal words usually begin reasoning?
check.why: This shows, therefore and this means introduce an explanation of what the evidence proves.

lessons.title: Tracing an Argument
lessons.mainIdea: To trace an argument, find the claim, list each piece of evidence, and check the reasoning that links them; then you can judge whether the argument holds.
reading: Someone hands you an editorial that argues for a later school start. Before you decide whether you agree, trace it. *Tracing* an argument means following its path: where does it start, what does it stand on, and how does it get to the end? Start by finding the claim. It is usually in the first or last paragraph, and it is the sentence everything else serves.

Next, number the evidence. Go paragraph by paragraph and mark each fact, statistic, example or expert quote. Write them as a list. An editorial might give: the doctors' recommendation, a district that changed its start time, a survey of students, and the writer's own memory of being tired. Four pieces. Now you can see the argument's skeleton instead of feeling its tone.

Then check each link. For each piece of evidence, ask: does the writer explain how it supports the claim? Does the explanation make sense? Some evidence will be strong and well connected. Some will be dropped in with no reasoning, or connected by a stretch. Mark those. An argument is only as strong as its weakest link that it relies on.

Finally, judge. Is the claim supported well enough to accept? You may agree with a claim and still find the argument weak, or disagree with a claim and admit the argument is solid. That is a sign of a fair reader. Tracing turns "I liked it" or "I did not" into "here is where it holds and here is where it breaks."

words.d: to follow an argument step by step from its claim through its evidence and reasoning
an article that gives an opinion and argues for it, often in a newspaper

look.title: Skeleton of an Editorial
look.text: Claim: the city should build more bike lanes. Evidence 1: a count showing bike traffic doubled on one street after a lane was added. Evidence 2: the writer's cousin says biking is fun. Evidence 3: a city report that bike lanes reduced crashes on three streets by a fifth. Evidence 4: many big cities have bike lanes.
look.prompt: Rank the four pieces of evidence from strongest to weakest. Which one needs the most reasoning to connect it to the claim?

check.q: What is the first step in tracing an argument?
check.why: The claim is what everything else serves, so you find it first.

check.q: Why should you write the evidence as a numbered list?
choices: So you can see the argument's structure instead of just feeling its tone
Because lists are required in essays
Because evidence is always numbered in editorials
check.why: Listing the evidence shows the skeleton of the argument so you can judge each piece.

check.q: Can you agree with a claim and still find the argument for it weak?
choices: No, agreeing means the argument is good
Only if the writer is famous
Yes, the claim and the quality of the argument are separate things
No, weak arguments always have false claims
check.why: A fair reader judges the support, not just the conclusion. A good claim can be argued badly.

lessons.title: Relevant and Sufficient
lessons.mainIdea: Evidence must be relevant, meaning it connects to the claim, and sufficient, meaning there is enough of it to carry the claim's weight.
reading: Marcus argued that a later start would cause bus problems. Suppose he had said: "Also, the school's football team won six games last year." True, maybe. But it has nothing to do with bus schedules. That evidence is not *relevant*. Relevant evidence connects to the claim. Irrelevant evidence is a distraction, and readers who notice it stop trusting the writer.

Relevance is not enough by itself. Suppose Priya's only evidence had been that she personally feels tired at 8:00. Relevant, yes. But one tired student is not enough to change a whole school's schedule. Her evidence would not be *sufficient*. Sufficient means enough, in amount and in strength, to hold up the claim. Big claims need more evidence than small ones.

How much is enough? Think about the size of the claim. "I should go to bed earlier" needs one piece of evidence: you are tired. "Every middle school in Illinois should start at 8:30" needs a lot: research on teen sleep, data from schools that changed, costs, effects on families. A writer who supports a huge claim with a single example is asking you to take a leap. Do not take it.

When you check an argument, or your own draft, ask both questions of every piece of evidence. Is it relevant: does it truly bear on the claim? Then step back and ask of the whole pile: is it sufficient: is there enough here, and is it strong enough, to convince a careful reader who does not already agree?

words.d: connected to the claim; having something to do with the point
enough in amount and strength to support a claim
not connected to the claim; off the point

look.title: Sort the Evidence
look.text: Claim: our school should replace paper worksheets with tablets. Evidence offered: A. The school printed 400,000 pages last year. B. Tablets come in many colors. C. A nearby school reported saving 9,000 dollars a year on paper after switching. D. The principal likes technology. E. A study of 2,000 students found no difference in test scores between paper and tablet work.
look.prompt: Which pieces are relevant? Of those, which help the claim and which hurt it? Is the relevant evidence sufficient?

check.q: Evidence that has nothing to do with the claim is called
check.why: Irrelevant evidence does not connect to the point. It distracts and weakens trust.

check.q: Why is one student's tiredness not sufficient evidence for changing a school's schedule?
choices: Because a big claim needs more and stronger evidence than one example
check.why: Sufficient means enough. One example cannot carry a claim about a whole school.

check.q: How does the size of a claim affect the evidence needed?
check.why: The larger the claim, the more weight the evidence must hold, so more and stronger evidence is needed.

lessons.title: Counterclaims and Rebuttal
lessons.mainIdea: A strong argument states the other side's best point fairly and then answers it; that answer is the rebuttal.
reading: Marcus did something Jalen never did. In the middle of his own argument he said, "Priya is right that sleep matters." Then he explained why he still disagreed. That move is a *counterclaim*: naming the opposing view. Some students fear that mentioning the other side makes them look weak. The opposite is true. A reader who already knows the objection and sees that you ignored it stops trusting you.

State the counterclaim fairly. Do not write "Some people think buses do not matter at all," if no one really thinks that. Write the strongest version: "Opponents point out that a later start would delay buses for elementary students and cost money the district does not have." Steel, not straw. If you can only beat a weak version of the other side, you have not really won.

Then answer it. The answer is the *rebuttal*. A rebuttal can show that the counterclaim is wrong (the buses could run on a two-tier schedule at no extra cost), that it is true but less important than the writer's point (bus schedules can be fixed; sleep loss harms health), or that it is true but does not lead to the conclusion the opponent wants. Use evidence in the rebuttal too, not just a louder voice.

A model, written for this lesson: "Some argue that a later start simply pushes students to stay up later. But when one district in Minnesota moved its bell an hour later, students' bedtimes stayed about the same and they gained most of that hour in sleep. The worry is reasonable, but the evidence does not support it." Counterclaim, stated fairly. Rebuttal, backed by evidence. That paragraph makes the whole argument stronger.

words.d: the opposing side's claim, stated inside your own argument
your answer to a counterclaim, showing why your position still holds

look.title: One Paragraph, Two Sides
look.text: Critics of the new recess plan say that thirty minutes outside will cut into math time. It is true that the schedule loses ten minutes of math. But teachers in the two classrooms that tried the plan last spring reported that students finished the same math lessons in less time because they were calmer and more focused after moving. Ten minutes lost on paper became time gained in practice.
look.cite: A model paragraph written for this lesson
look.prompt: Which sentence is the counterclaim? Which sentences are the rebuttal? Does the rebuttal say the critics are wrong, or that they are right about something smaller than they think?

check.q: Why should a writer include a counterclaim?
choices: Because readers who know the objection will distrust a writer who ignores it
To show the writer has no opinion
check.why: Naming and answering the other side shows fairness and earns the reader's trust.

check.q: What does it mean to state the counterclaim as steel, not straw?
choices: To write it in bold letters
To give the strongest fair version of the opposing view
To make it sound silly so it is easy to beat
check.why: Beating a weak version of the other side proves nothing. A fair, strong version makes your rebuttal mean something.

check.q: A rebuttal should rely on
check.why: A rebuttal is part of the argument, so it needs evidence and reasoning like everything else.

lessons.title: Three Fallacies to Spot
lessons.mainIdea: A fallacy is a mistake in reasoning that makes an argument sound good without really supporting it; bandwagon, ad hominem and false choice are three of the most common.
reading: Jalen said three things that sounded like reasons but were not. "Everyone is tired." "Ask anybody." "Anyone who disagrees has never been a kid." Each one is a *fallacy*: a pattern of bad reasoning that feels convincing but proves nothing. Learning a few fallacies by name is like learning the tricks of a card sharp. Once you can see the move, it stops working on you.

*Bandwagon* is the claim that something is right because many people believe it or do it. "Everyone agrees school starts too early." Even if everyone did agree, that would not make it true; crowds have been wrong before. The fix is to ask for the reason behind the crowd's belief, not the size of the crowd. *Ad hominem* is Latin for "to the person." It attacks the speaker instead of the argument. "Anyone who disagrees has never been a kid." That says nothing about buses, budgets or sleep. It just tries to shame the other side into silence.

*False choice* pretends there are only two options when there are more. "Either we start school at nine or students keep failing." Really? Maybe school could start at 8:30. Maybe first period could be a study hall. Whenever someone says "either this or that," look for a third door. There almost always is one.

Fallacies are not always lies. The person using one may believe every word. But a fallacy is still a hole in the argument, and a careful reader or judge will walk right through it. In your own writing, hunt for them before someone else does. In a debate, name them politely: "That is an attack on the speaker, not on the idea."

words.d: a mistake in reasoning that makes an argument seem stronger than it is
the fallacy of claiming something is right because many people believe it
the fallacy of attacking the person instead of answering the argument
the fallacy of pretending there are only two options when there are more

look.title: Name the Fallacy
look.text: A. "Every popular kid in eighth grade has this phone, so it must be the best." B. "Either we cancel homework or students will burn out by tenth grade." C. "Why listen to the librarian about screen time? She is fifty years old." D. "Everybody knows the cafeteria pizza is the worst in the city."
look.prompt: Match each sentence to bandwagon, ad hominem or false choice. Then rewrite one of them as a real argument with evidence.

check.q: "Everyone agrees, so it must be true." Which fallacy is this?
check.why: Bandwagon treats the size of the crowd as proof. Popularity is not evidence.

check.q: "Anyone who disagrees has never been a kid." What is wrong with this?
choices: It attacks the person instead of answering the argument
check.why: This is ad hominem. It shames the speaker and says nothing about the actual question.

check.q: What is the best response to a false choice?
choices: Look for a third option the speaker left out
check.why: A false choice hides other options. Naming a third possibility exposes the fallacy.

lessons.title: The Shape of the Essay
lessons.mainIdea: An argumentative essay has an introduction with a claim, body paragraphs that each give evidence and reasoning, a counterclaim paragraph with a rebuttal, and a conclusion.
reading: An argumentative essay is Priya's speech, written down and built bigger. Its shape is simple enough to draw. Introduction: a hook, some background, and the claim. Body paragraph one: first reason, with evidence and reasoning. Body paragraph two: second reason, same shape. Counterclaim paragraph: the other side, stated fairly, then the rebuttal. Conclusion: the claim restated in fresh words and a reason the reader should care. Five paragraphs is a fine place to start, not a law.

The *introduction* earns the reader's attention. A hook might be a short scene, a striking number or a question. "At 7:40 on a January morning, half the students in first period have their heads on their desks." Then a sentence or two of background so a reader who knows nothing can follow. Then the claim, in one clear sentence, usually last in the paragraph.

Each *body paragraph* follows a pattern. Topic sentence naming the reason. Evidence with its source. Reasoning that connects the evidence to the claim. A closing sentence that ties back. The paragraph on the doctors' recommendation and the paragraph on the class survey are separate paragraphs because they are separate reasons. One reason per paragraph keeps the reader from getting lost.

The *conclusion* is not a copy of the introduction. Restate the claim in new words, remind the reader of the strongest point, and then answer the question so what: why does this matter beyond this essay? "A later bell would not just make mornings easier. It would give seven hundred students back an hour of sleep their brains need to grow." End on the reason, not on "in conclusion."

words.d: the opening paragraph of an essay, with a hook, background and the claim
a middle paragraph that gives one reason with its evidence and reasoning
the last paragraph, which restates the claim in new words and says why it matters

look.title: Sentences per Paragraph in a Model Essay
look.cite: A five-paragraph model essay on school start times, written and counted for this lesson
look.prompt: Why are the body paragraphs the longest? What has to fit inside each one?

check.q: Where does the claim usually appear in an argumentative essay?
choices: At the end of the introduction
check.why: The introduction hooks the reader, gives background and then states the claim, usually as its last sentence.

check.q: Why should each body paragraph cover only one reason?
choices: Because essays must have exactly five paragraphs
Because one reason per paragraph keeps the reader from getting lost
check.why: One reason per paragraph gives each reason room for its evidence and reasoning and keeps the structure clear.

check.q: What should a conclusion do?
choices: Copy the introduction word for word
Restate the claim in new words and say why it matters
check.why: A conclusion answers so what. It restates the claim freshly and points to why the reader should care.

lessons.title: Transitions and a Formal Voice
lessons.mainIdea: Transitions show the reader how ideas connect, and a formal style keeps the focus on the argument instead of on the writer's feelings.
reading: Read these sentences with nothing between them. "Doctors recommend an 8:30 start. Our school starts at 8:00. Many students are absent from first period." True, but the reader has to guess how they connect. Now add *transitions*: "Doctors recommend an 8:30 start. However, our school starts at 8:00. As a result, many students are absent from first period." Two words, and the logic is visible.

Different transitions do different jobs. To add: also, in addition, furthermore. To contrast: however, on the other hand, although. To show cause: because, therefore, as a result, consequently. To give an example: for instance, for example. To concede a point: admittedly, it is true that. To conclude: in the end, ultimately. Pick the one that names the real connection. A wrong transition is worse than none.

*Formal style* means writing for a reader you do not know, who will judge your argument by its words. Drop slang and texting habits. Avoid "I think" and "in my opinion"; the whole essay is your opinion, so just state the claim. Avoid "you" when you mean people in general. Do not shout with exclamation points or all caps. Formal does not mean stiff or full of big words. It means clear, calm and confident.

Compare. Informal: "Honestly, starting at 8 is crazy and everybody knows it!!" Formal: "An 8:00 start conflicts with the sleep needs that pediatricians have described." The second sentence is not fancier. It is calmer, it points to evidence, and it would not embarrass you in front of a school board. That is the voice an argument deserves.

words.d: a word or phrase that shows how one idea connects to the next
clear, calm writing for readers you do not know, without slang or personal chatter
to admit that a point on the other side is true

look.title: Same Paragraph, Two Voices
look.text: Informal: So basically the buses are a huge problem, and I think the district is being kind of lazy about it. Formal: The bus schedule is a real obstacle. Admittedly, the district has limited funds; however, a two-tier schedule, which several nearby districts already use, would solve the problem without new spending.
look.cite: Two versions written for this lesson
look.prompt: List every change between the two versions. Which transitions does the formal version use, and what job does each one do?

check.q: Which transition shows a contrast?
check.why: However signals that the next idea pushes against the one before it.

check.q: Why should a writer avoid "I think" in a formal argument?
choices: Because the whole essay is already the writer's view, so stating the claim directly is stronger
check.why: The essay is the writer's opinion. Saying "I think" adds nothing and sounds less sure.

check.q: What does formal style mean?
choices: Clear, calm writing without slang for a reader you do not know
check.why: Formal style is about clarity and calm, not fancy words. It keeps the focus on the argument.

lessons.title: How a Classroom Debate Runs
lessons.mainIdea: A debate is an argument with rules: two sides, timed turns, a stated resolution, and judges who score evidence and reasoning rather than volume.
reading: A shouting match is not a debate. A *debate* is an argument with a shape. First, a *resolution*: the claim being argued, written so it can be supported or opposed. "Resolved: this school should start no earlier than 8:30." One side, the affirmative, argues for it. The other, the negative, argues against it. The sides are assigned, not chosen. You may have to argue a view you do not hold, which is excellent practice in fairness.

Then, timed turns. A simple format: each side gives an opening statement of two minutes, laying out its claim and main evidence. Then each side gives a rebuttal of one minute, answering the other's points. Then a closing of one minute each. A timekeeper calls time. No interruptions. While the other side speaks, you take notes on what you will answer. Listening is half the job.

Judges do not vote on which side they agree with. They score with a rubric: was the claim clear? Was the evidence specific and sourced? Did the reasoning connect? Did the rebuttal actually answer the other side, or just repeat the opening? Was the speaker respectful? Jalen lost because his column was empty, not because the class disliked him.

The rules are what make a debate useful. They force both sides to prepare evidence, to listen, and to answer instead of interrupt. Adults who never learned this argue on the internet in all caps. Students who learn it can walk into a school board meeting and be heard.

words.d: a formal argument between two sides with rules, timed turns and judges
the claim being debated, written so one side supports it and the other opposes it
a scoring guide that lists what judges look for and how many points each part earns

look.title: A Debate Rubric
look.cite: A classroom rubric written for this lesson
look.prompt: Delivery is worth only 3 points out of 25. Why do you think the rubric puts so much more weight on evidence, reasoning and rebuttal?

check.q: What is a resolution in a debate?
choices: The claim being argued, written so it can be supported or opposed
check.why: The resolution is the debate's claim. The affirmative supports it and the negative opposes it.

check.q: What should judges base their scores on?
choices: Which side they personally agree with
The clarity of the claim, the evidence, the reasoning and the rebuttal
Which side had more friends in the room
check.why: Judges score the quality of the argument with a rubric, not their own opinion of the topic.

check.q: Why might you be assigned to argue a side you disagree with?
choices: To practice fairness and understand the other view
Because the teacher wants you to lose
Because your opinion does not matter
check.why: Arguing the other side builds fairness and shows you the strongest version of the opposing case.

lessons.title: Listening and Answering
lessons.mainIdea: In a debate the rebuttal turn is won by listening closely, writing down the other side's exact points, and answering them one by one with evidence.
reading: The most common debate mistake is easy to spot. A speaker stands up for the rebuttal and simply repeats the opening statement, a little louder. Nothing the other side said gets answered. Judges notice. A *rebuttal* turn is for answering, and you cannot answer what you did not hear. So the real work of the rebuttal happens while the other side is speaking.

Use a two-column sheet. Left column: what they said, in short notes. "Buses cost money. 140 students have jobs. Fix screens, not the bell." Right column: your answer to each, with the evidence you will use. "Two-tier bus schedule, no new cost. Jobs start at 4:00, school would end at 3:30. Screen limits and a later bell can both happen." When you stand up, go down the list. "My opponent made three points. First..."

Answer the strongest point first, not the weakest. Judges are waiting to see if you can handle it. If you honestly cannot answer a point, *concede* it and explain why your side still wins: "It is true that a later start will cost the district some money. But the health of seven hundred students is worth more than a bus schedule." A calm concession is more convincing than a dodge.

Keep your tone respectful. Say "my opponent argued" and never "that is stupid." Refer to their evidence, not their character; an ad hominem in a debate costs you points and trust. Finish your rebuttal by returning to your own claim in one sentence, so the judges leave your turn remembering what you stand for.

words.d: the part of a debate when each side answers the other side's points
the person or side arguing against you in a debate

look.title: Two Rebuttals
