look.text: The negative side argued that a later start would end the day too late for students with jobs. Rebuttal A: "Like I said, doctors say we need sleep, and sleep is really important, so we should start later." Rebuttal B: "My opponent says a 3:30 end would hurt students with jobs. But the counselor's list shows most student jobs begin at 4:00 or later, so a 3:30 end leaves time to get there."
look.prompt: Which rebuttal would score higher, and why? What did the weaker one fail to do?

check.q: What is the most common rebuttal mistake?
choices: Repeating the opening statement instead of answering the other side
check.why: A rebuttal must answer what the other side said. Repeating your opening answers nothing.

check.q: Why should you answer the other side's strongest point first?
choices: Because judges want to see you handle it
Because weak points cannot be answered
check.why: Judges are watching to see whether you can meet the toughest objection. Facing it first shows confidence.

check.q: When you honestly cannot answer a point, the best move is to
choices: change the subject to a fallacy
concede it and explain why your side still wins
check.why: A calm concession keeps your credibility. A dodge or an attack loses it.

review.q: Which of these is a strong claim?
choices: Middle schools should start no earlier than 8:30
Many people have opinions about school hours
review.why: A strong claim is specific, arguable and supportable. The others are facts, near-facts or fence-sitting.

review.q: Why did Jalen's argument get only three votes?
choices: He gave no evidence or reasoning, only fallacies
review.why: The class agreed with his claim but he never supported it. Judges score evidence and reasoning.

review.q: What is the job of reasoning in an argument?
choices: To explain how the evidence supports the claim
review.why: Reasoning is the bridge between evidence and claim. Without it, the reader asks so what.

review.q: Evidence that is connected to the claim but too thin to support it is
review.why: Relevant means connected; sufficient means enough. Evidence can be one without the other.

review.q: "Either we cancel homework or students will burn out." Which fallacy is this?
review.why: The sentence pretends there are only two options. There are many others, such as less homework.

review.q: What is a rebuttal?
review.why: A rebuttal answers the counterclaim and shows why the writer's position still holds.

review.q: Which sentence uses a transition to show cause?
choices: In addition, the buses run late
As a result, first period has the most absences
For example, the buses run late
review.why: As a result signals that one thing caused another.

review.q: In a classroom debate, judges score
choices: the clarity of claims, evidence, reasoning and rebuttal
review.why: A rubric scores the quality of the argument, not the judge's own opinion or the speaker's volume.

chapters.title: Media and Sources
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you find out whether something you read or see online is true, and how do you use it honestly in your own work?

story.title: Three Captions, One Photo
story.kicker: A picture of a flooded street races across phones with three different stories attached. Only one student goes looking for where it came from.
paragraphs: On a Tuesday in April, a photo lands in a group chat of eighth graders on Chicago's Northwest Side. It shows a street under brown water up to the car doors, a stop sign leaning, a man wading with a dog on his shoulders. The first caption says: "Milwaukee Avenue right now, the city did NOTHING." Within an hour it has been sent to half the school.

By lunch a second version is going around. Same photo, new caption: "This is what climate change looks like in our neighborhood." By afternoon a third: "Fake. This is from Texas in 2017, people will believe anything." Three captions, three stories, and now the chat is a shouting match. Everyone is sure. Nobody has checked.

Rosa is not sure. She saves the photo and runs an image search on it. The oldest match she finds is a local news site from four years earlier. The street is real and it is in Chicago, but it is on the South Side, not Milwaukee Avenue. The article says a water main broke, the city closed the street within an hour, and crews fixed it by the next morning. The man with the dog is quoted by name.

Rosa posts the link. "It's real, but it's four years old, it's a broken pipe, and the city fixed it in a day." The chat goes quiet. Then someone asks: "How did you find that?" She explains: search the image, find the oldest version, read the original source, then compare it with the captions. Twenty minutes of work. Three captions were wrong, each in its own way.

The first caption used a true picture to tell a false story about neglect. The second used it to argue about a cause it had nothing to do with. The third called it fake, which was also wrong. Rosa did not have special tools or special knowledge. She had a habit: before you believe or share, find out where it came from. This chapter is about that habit, and about using what you find honestly in your own work.
story.think: Each of the three captions was wrong in a different way. Which one do you think was most harmful, and why? What made Rosa's answer more trustworthy than any of them?

lessons.title: Who Made This, and Why?
lessons.mainIdea: Before trusting a source, find out who made it and what they wanted from you, because author and purpose shape everything in it.
reading: Two web pages both say that a certain energy drink is safe for teenagers. One is written by a doctor at a children's hospital. The other is the energy drink company's own site. Same claim, very different weight. The first question to ask of any *source* is: who made this? The second is: why? Together, author and *purpose* tell you how much to trust what follows.

Finding the author takes a little digging. Look for a name at the top or bottom of the page. Click About or About Us. Look at the web address: .gov is a government site, .edu is a school or university, .org is often a nonprofit but anyone can buy one, .com is a business or anyone at all. If you cannot find out who made a page, that is itself a warning sign.

Purpose comes in a few common forms. To inform: a museum page explaining the Chicago Fire. To persuade: an editorial arguing for later school start times. To sell: a page that ends with a Buy Now button. To entertain: a joke site. To get clicks: a headline that promises shock and delivers nothing. A source built to sell or to get clicks can still contain facts, but every fact in it was chosen to serve that purpose.

Ask a third question too: what does the author know? A doctor writing about a drink's effect on the heart knows more than a celebrity who was paid to hold the can. Expertise is not fame. A source with a named author who has real knowledge of the subject, and a clear purpose to inform, is the kind you want at the top of your list.

words.d: any text, image, video or person that information comes from
the reason a source was made: to inform, persuade, sell, entertain or get attention
deep knowledge of a subject gained through training or experience

look.title: Four Pages About One Drink
look.text: Page A: The drink company's site, no author named, ends with a coupon. Page B: A children's hospital page written by a named heart doctor. Page C: A blog by a teenager who loves the drink. Page D: A news article from last month quoting two doctors and the company's spokesperson.
look.prompt: Rank the four pages by how much you would trust them on whether the drink is safe. What is the purpose of each?

check.q: What are the first two questions to ask of any source?
choices: How long is it, and does it have pictures?
Is it popular, and is it recent?
Does it agree with me, and is it free?
check.why: Author and purpose shape everything else in a source, so they come first.

check.q: A page has no author's name anywhere and no About page. What does that suggest?
choices: The page is probably a government site
The page is written by an expert
That is a warning sign about the source
check.why: Trustworthy sources say who made them. A missing author makes the source harder to trust.

check.q: Why does a company's own page about its product deserve extra caution?
choices: Because its purpose is to sell, so every fact was chosen to serve that goal
Because companies never tell the truth
check.why: A page built to sell can contain facts, but it selects them to persuade you to buy.

lessons.title: Date and Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: A good source is recent enough for its topic and shows where its own facts came from; check both before you rely on it.
reading: Rosa's photo was real. It was also four years old. For a claim about what is happening "right now," the *date* is everything. For some topics, age matters less: a page about the Chicago Fire written in 2005 may be fine. For others, it matters a lot: a page about phone safety, a disease, or a city budget can be wrong within a year. Look for the date the source was published or last updated. If there is none, be careful.

Then look at the source's own evidence. Does the writer say where the facts came from? A strong source names studies, reports, people with expertise, or documents you could find yourself. "Studies show" with no study named is a weak sign. So is a page that is all claims and no numbers, or all numbers and no source for them. A source that shows its evidence is inviting you to check, which is what honest writers do.

Here is a model passage written for this lesson. "The Lakeside County road department reported that crews filled 412 potholes during the first week of March 2023, according to a county press release." The county is invented, but notice the parts: a named department, a number, a specific time, and a document you could look for. Compare: "Tons of pipes broke that winter, everyone knows the city is falling apart." Nothing there can be checked.

Put author, purpose, date and evidence together and you have a simple checklist. Who made it? Why? When? How do they know? A source that answers all four clearly is worth using. A source that fails two of them may still be worth a look, but not worth building an argument on.

words.d: when a source was published or last updated
an official statement an organization sends to the news
a short list of things to check, one by one

look.title: How Fast Topics Go Stale
rows: Number of students in a school
look.cite: Rough estimates written for this lesson, for discussion
look.prompt: Why does a history page stay useful longer than a phone review? Can you think of a topic where even a one-year-old source would be too old?

check.q: For which topic does the date of a source matter most?
choices: The causes of the Chicago Fire
The current price of a phone
The plot of a novel from 1876
check.why: Prices change quickly, so a source about them goes stale fast. History and old rules change slowly.

check.q: "Studies show that the drink is safe." What is missing?
choices: Which studies, so a reader could check them
check.why: Naming the study is what makes the claim checkable. Without it, the sentence is a weak sign.

check.q: What is the four-part checklist for judging a source?
choices: Who, why, when, and how do they know
check.why: Author, purpose, date and evidence are the four questions to ask of every source.

lessons.title: Reading Sideways
lessons.mainIdea: Lateral reading means leaving a source to check what other, independent sources say about it, which is faster and more reliable than judging a page by its own looks.
reading: A page about a health claim looks great: clean design, charts, a long list of references, an About page full of doctors' names. Is it trustworthy? Staring at the page cannot tell you. A polished look is easy to buy. What professional fact checkers do instead is leave the page. They open a new tab and search for the organization's name. That habit is called *lateral reading*: reading sideways, across other sources, instead of straight down one page.

Here is how it works. You land on a site called, say, the Institute for Nutrition Freedom. Instead of reading its articles, you search the name. You find that a news organization reported the institute is funded by a supplement company. You find a science site that says the institute's claims contradict most research. In two minutes you know more about the source than an hour on its own pages would tell you.

Lateral reading answers questions a page will never answer about itself. Who funds this? What do others who know the subject say about it? Has it been wrong before? Is this organization what it claims to be? A source that turns out to be respected by independent experts rises in your list. A source that only praises itself sinks.

Rosa read laterally with a photo. She did not ask whether the picture looked real; she searched for where it came from. The same move works for a quote, a statistic or a shocking claim: search for the claim itself, plus a word like fact check, and see what independent sources say. Independent means not connected to the source you are checking.

words.d: checking a source by looking at what other, independent sources say about it
not connected to or paid by the source being checked
a person whose job is to test whether claims are true

look.title: Two Students, One Website
look.text: Both students land on a site claiming a new study proves video games raise math scores. Student A reads the whole site, admires the charts, and notes that it lists twelve references. Student B searches the site's name and the study's title in a new tab and finds that the study was paid for by a game company and that two university researchers say its method was flawed.
look.prompt: Who learned more about whether to trust the site, and in less time? What could Student A never have discovered by staying on the page?

check.q: What is lateral reading?
choices: Reading a page from top to bottom very carefully
Leaving a source to see what independent sources say about it
check.why: Lateral reading means opening other tabs to check on a source rather than judging it by its own pages.

check.q: Why is a polished design not proof that a source is trustworthy?
choices: Because trustworthy sites are always ugly
Because a professional look is easy to buy and says nothing about accuracy
check.why: Anyone can make a page look good. Accuracy has to be checked another way.

check.q: An independent source is one that
choices: is not connected to or paid by the source being checked
check.why: Independence is what makes another source useful for checking. A connected source cannot be a fair check.

lessons.title: Bias and Point of View
lessons.mainIdea: Every source comes from a perspective, and bias is when that perspective bends what is reported; spotting it means asking what was left out and how it was worded.
reading: Two websites report the same school board vote. One headline: "Board Slashes Arts Budget." The other: "Board Trims Spending to Protect Teacher Jobs." The vote was real. The numbers match. But each site chose a verb, a focus and a frame that pushes you toward one feeling. That push is *bias*: a leaning that shapes how facts are chosen and worded.

Bias is not the same as lying, and it is not always deliberate. Every writer stands somewhere. A parent of an art student and a teacher afraid of layoffs will notice different things in the same meeting. That is *perspective*, and it is unavoidable. Bias is what happens when perspective starts leaving things out or loading the words. The question is never "is this source biased?" It is "how much, in which direction, and what did it leave out?"

Three ways to spot bias. Word choice: slashes versus trims, mob versus crowd, admits versus says. Selection: which facts made it in, and which did not? A story on the arts cut that never mentions the teacher jobs is leaving something out. Sources quoted: does the writer quote only one side? A fair report gives the other side a voice; a biased one gives it a sentence at the end or nothing at all.

You do not have to throw out a biased source. You have to read it knowing where it leans, and then read another one leaning the other way. Put "Board Slashes Arts Budget" next to "Board Trims Spending" and you can see the shape of what actually happened better than either one shows alone. That is the same skill as comparing two accounts of the Chicago Fire.

words.d: a leaning for or against something that shapes how facts are chosen and worded
the position a person sees from, shaped by who they are and what they care about
the choice of which facts and voices to include and which to leave out

look.title: One Vote, Two Reports
look.text: Report A: The board slashed the arts budget by 80,000 dollars Tuesday night, ignoring dozens of students who begged them to reconsider. Report B: Facing a shortfall, the board reduced arts spending by 80,000 dollars Tuesday, a move officials said would prevent the layoff of three teachers. Students spoke against the cut.
look.cite: Two versions written for this lesson
look.prompt: Underline every word that differs. What does each report leave out that the other includes? Which one gives a voice to both sides?

check.q: "Board Slashes Arts Budget" and "Board Trims Spending" describe the same vote. What is the difference?
choices: Word choice pushes the reader toward different feelings
One is about a different school
check.why: Slashes and trims are the same fact with different connotations. That is bias through word choice.

check.q: Which of these is a sign of bias through selection?
choices: A report that gives both sides a voice
A report that names its author
A report that never mentions the other side's main reason
check.why: Leaving out the other side's reason is choosing which facts count, which is selection bias.

check.q: What should you do with a biased source?
choices: Read it knowing where it leans, and read one leaning the other way
Trust it if it agrees with you
check.why: Biased sources still carry facts. Reading across leanings shows the shape of what happened.

lessons.title: What a Headline and a Photo Do
lessons.mainIdea: Headlines and images are chosen to grab you before you read, so check whether they match what the article actually says and where the picture really came from.
reading: Most people read the headline and the picture, and nothing else. Writers and editors know this. So a *headline* is written to grab: "City Did NOTHING as Street Floods." Then the article, three paragraphs down, says crews arrived within an hour. The headline and the story disagree. This gap is so common that it has a name: clickbait. A headline is a promise. Always check whether the article keeps it.

Images work even faster than headlines. A photo of a flooded street with a man carrying a dog makes you feel something before you think anything. That feeling gets attached to whatever caption sits under the picture. Rosa's photo carried three different stories and never changed. The picture did not lie. The captions did. When a picture makes you feel strongly, that is the moment to slow down.

Ask four questions about an image. Where did it come from? An image search finds the earliest version. When was it taken? Old pictures get reused for new events all the time. What is outside the frame? A crowd shot can be tight or wide. Has it been changed? Edits, crops and now computer-made pictures are common, and a picture that seems too perfect for its story may have been made for it.

Try this with a photo you see this week. Cover the caption and write your own. Then uncover it. If the caption tells you what to feel instead of what you are seeing, someone is doing your thinking for you. Do the same with a headline: read the article, then write the headline you would have written. Compare.

words.d: the large title above an article, written to grab a reader's attention
a headline or image that promises more than the content delivers, to get clicks
searching the web with a picture instead of words to find where it appeared before

look.title: Where Readers Stop
rows: Read the headline and first paragraph
look.cite: A classroom survey about one shared article, written for this lesson
look.prompt: More than half the class stopped at the headline. If the headline and the article disagreed, what would most of the class believe?

check.q: What is clickbait?
choices: A headline or image that promises more than the article delivers
check.why: Clickbait grabs attention with a promise the content does not keep.

check.q: Why did Rosa's photo tell three different stories?
choices: The photo was edited three times
The captions changed while the photo stayed the same
check.why: A picture gets its meaning from its caption. Three captions made one true photo tell three tales.

check.q: What does an image search help you find?
choices: The earliest version of a picture and where it appeared
check.why: Searching with the image finds earlier copies, which shows when and where it really came from.

lessons.title: Paraphrase or Plagiarism?
lessons.mainIdea: Paraphrasing means restating a source's idea fully in your own words and structure and still giving credit; copying words or just swapping a few is plagiarism.
reading: A source says: "The Water Tower survived the 1871 fire because its limestone walls did not burn, and it became a symbol of the rebuilt city." A student writes: "The Water Tower lived through the 1871 fire because its limestone walls did not catch fire, and it turned into a symbol of the rebuilt city." Three words changed. This is not the student's writing. It is the source's sentence in a thin disguise. That is *plagiarism*, even if it feels like work.

Plagiarism means presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own. Copying a sentence is plagiarism. Swapping a few words is plagiarism. Using someone's idea without saying where it came from is plagiarism too, even in your own words. Schools take it seriously, and so does the adult world: writers, scientists and students have lost jobs and degrees over it. But the fix is simple, and it is a skill.

A real *paraphrase* starts by closing the source. Read the sentence, understand it, look away, then say it the way you would tell a friend. "Because the Water Tower was built of stone, it was one of the few buildings still standing after the fire, and Chicagoans came to see it as a sign of their city's comeback." New words, new order, same idea. Then, and this is the part students forget, you still give credit, because the idea came from the source.

Test your paraphrase. Put it next to the original. Are there three or more words in a row that match? Rewrite. Is the sentence shape the same? Rewrite. Could you explain the idea with the source hidden? If yes, it is yours to state, with credit. A paraphrase shows you understood. A copy only shows you could type.

words.d: presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own
to restate a source's idea in your own words and sentence structure, with credit
naming the source an idea or fact came from

look.title: Which One Is a Real Paraphrase?
look.text: Source: "Rip currents form when waves push water against the shore and it rushes back out through a narrow channel." Version 1: Rip currents form when waves shove water against the beach and it rushes back through a narrow channel. Version 2: When waves pile water up on a beach, that water has to escape, and it sometimes escapes in a narrow, fast-moving stream called a rip current.
look.prompt: Which version is a real paraphrase and which is plagiarism? Name the matching words in the weaker one. Does either version still need to credit the source?

check.q: A student copies a sentence and changes three words. What is this?
check.why: Swapping a few words leaves the source's writing in disguise. That is plagiarism.

check.q: What is the first step of a real paraphrase?
choices: Copy the sentence and then edit it
Understand the idea, then close the source and restate it
check.why: Looking away from the source forces you to use your own words and structure.

check.q: You paraphrase an idea perfectly in your own words. Do you still need to credit the source?
choices: No, your own words make it yours
Only if it is a quotation
Yes, because the idea still came from the source
check.why: Credit goes to ideas, not just words. A paraphrased idea still needs its source named.

lessons.title: Quoting Well
lessons.mainIdea: Quote when the exact words matter, keep quotations short, put them in quotation marks, and add an in-text citation so a reader can find the source.
reading: Sometimes the source's exact words are the point. A doctor's precise recommendation. A witness's vivid phrase. A sentence so well made that changing it would weaken it. Then you *quote*: copy the words exactly, put them inside quotation marks, and tell the reader where they came from. Quoting is not cheating. It is borrowing with a receipt.

Keep quotations short and make them work. Introduce the quote so the reader knows who is speaking: "The report warns that" or "According to the hospital's page," and then the words. After the quote, explain it in your own sentence. A quotation dropped into a paragraph with no introduction and no explanation is called a floating quote, and it reads as if the writer had nothing to say.

The receipt is the *in-text citation*. In MLA style, the style most English classes use, it is the author's last name and a page number in parentheses at the end of the sentence, before the period. Written for this lesson: The city's report states that crews "closed the street within an hour of the break" (Alvarez 4). If there is no page number, as on most websites, use just the name: (Alvarez). If there is no author, use a short form of the title in quotation marks.

Two habits keep you honest. First, copy the words exactly, including odd spelling, and if you cut part of a sentence, show it with three spaced dots. Second, never change the meaning by cutting. If the source said "the plan will not work," quoting "the plan will work" is not a quotation; it is a lie with quotation marks around it.

words.d: to copy a source's exact words inside quotation marks and give credit
the short note in parentheses that tells which source a quote or idea came from
a set of rules for citing sources, used in most English classes

look.title: Three Ways to Handle One Sentence
look.text: Source sentence, by a writer named Alvarez, page 4: Crews closed the street within an hour of the break and finished repairs by morning. Floating: "Crews closed the street within an hour of the break." Well introduced: The city's own report says that "crews closed the street within an hour of the break" (Alvarez 4), which shows the response was fast, not slow. Paraphrased: According to the city's report, workers shut the street within an hour and had it fixed by the next day (Alvarez 4).
look.cite: A model source and three uses of it, written for this lesson
look.prompt: Why is the floating quote weaker than the introduced one? Notice that the paraphrase still has a citation. Why?

check.q: When should you quote instead of paraphrase?
choices: When you do not understand the source
check.why: Quote when the precise wording carries the meaning. Otherwise a paraphrase usually reads better.

check.q: In MLA style, what goes in the parentheses after a quotation from a book?
choices: The author's last name and the page number
check.why: An MLA in-text citation is the author's last name and page number, such as (Alvarez 4).

check.q: What is a floating quote?
choices: A quotation dropped in with no introduction or explanation
A quotation longer than four lines
check.why: A floating quote is not introduced or explained, so it reads as if the writer had nothing to add.

lessons.title: The Works Cited Page
lessons.mainIdea: A works cited page lists every source you used, in alphabetical order, in a set format, so any reader can find what you found.
reading: The in-text citation says (Alvarez 4). The reader wonders: who is Alvarez? The answer is on the last page of your paper, the *works cited*. It is a list of every source you quoted or paraphrased, in alphabetical order by the author's last name. Each entry gives enough for a reader to find the source. Think of it as the map to your evidence.

In MLA style, the entries follow patterns. A book: Author's last name, first name. Title of the Book in italics. Publisher, year. Written for this lesson: Alvarez, Maria. Water Under the City. Lakeside Press, 2021. A web page: Author's last name, first name. "Title of the Page" in quotation marks. Name of the Website in italics, day month year, web address. Written for this lesson: Chen, David. "How a Water Main Breaks." City Pipes Explained, 3 Mar. 2022, citypipes.example.

Notice the order and the punctuation. Periods separate the big parts. The title of a whole book or website is in italics; the title of a page or article inside something bigger goes in quotation marks. The first line of each entry starts at the margin and the following lines are indented. This is called a hanging indent, and it makes the alphabetical list easy to scan.

You will not memorize every pattern, and you do not have to. Keep a model handy, or use a citation tool, and then check the tool's result against the pattern, because tools make mistakes. What you must remember is the purpose: every source you leaned on appears here, so a reader can retrace your steps. A research paper with no works cited is a paper with no receipts.

words.d: the alphabetical list at the end of a paper of every source used in it
a format where the first line of an entry starts at the margin and the rest are indented
one item in a list, such as one source in a works cited

look.title: Put Them in Order
look.text: A student used four sources: a book by Maria Alvarez; a web page by David Chen; a news article by Sarah Baker with no page numbers; and a museum page with no author, titled "The Fire of 1871." The student's works cited lists them in the order she found them: Chen, Alvarez, the museum page, Baker.
look.prompt: What order should they be in? Where does an entry with no author go, and what would its in-text citation look like?

check.q: How is a works cited page ordered?
choices: By the order you found the sources
By how much you used each source
Alphabetically by the author's last name
check.why: Alphabetical order by last name lets a reader find any entry quickly from the in-text citation.

check.q: In MLA style, which title goes in quotation marks?
choices: An article or page inside a bigger website or book
check.why: Titles of parts, like articles and pages, take quotation marks. Whole works, like books and sites, take italics.

check.q: What is the purpose of a works cited page?
choices: To let a reader find every source you used
To show off how many books you own
check.why: The list is the map to your evidence. It lets any reader retrace your steps.

lessons.title: A Question and Good Notes
lessons.mainIdea: Research starts with a question that is narrow enough to answer, and note cards that keep the source, the fact and your own thinking separate.
reading: "I want to research water." That is a topic, and it would take a lifetime. Research starts with a *research question*: something specific enough that a few good sources could answer it. "Why do Chicago's water mains break in winter, and what is the city doing about it?" Now you know what to look for. A good question is narrow. It can be answered with sources you can find. And it interests you enough to carry you through the work.

Then gather sources with the checklist from this chapter: who, why, when, how do they know. Aim for three to five sources of different kinds: a news article, a government or museum page, a book or encyclopedia entry, maybe an interview with someone who knows. If every source says the same thing, good. If they disagree, even better; that disagreement may become the most interesting part of your paper.

Take *notes* in a way that protects you from accidental plagiarism. Each note has three parts. First, where it came from, with the page or web address. Second, the fact or idea, in your own words. If you copy exact words, put them in quotation marks. Third, your own thought about it, marked so you can tell it apart later. Many students use a different color or a label like ME for their own ideas. Later, you will thank yourself.

A note written for this lesson: Source: Chen, "How a Water Main Breaks," 2022. Fact: old cast iron pipes get brittle in cold and crack when the ground shifts. Quote: "Some of Chicago's pipes are more than a century old." ME: so the age of the pipes might matter more than the weather. That last line is the start of a claim. Research questions turn into claims exactly this way.

words.d: a specific question that guides a research project and that sources can answer
short records of facts, quotes and ideas from sources, with where each came from
focused on one small part of a topic rather than the whole thing

look.title: Narrow the Question
look.text: Three students write questions. Amir: "What is the history of Chicago?" Bea: "Why did the Chicago Fire spread so fast, and what did the city change afterward?" Cal: "Was the Chicago Fire bad?"
look.prompt: Which question is narrow enough to research but big enough to matter? What is wrong with each of the other two?

check.q: Which of these is a good research question?
choices: Why do Chicago's water mains break in winter, and what is the city doing about it?
check.why: A good research question is specific, answerable with sources and interesting. The others are topics or yes-or-no questions.

check.q: Why should each note record where the fact came from?
choices: So you can cite it later and avoid accidental plagiarism
So you can throw the source away
check.why: Notes with sources let you cite correctly and keep your words separate from the source's.

check.q: Your sources disagree with each other. What should you do?
choices: Pick the one you like and ignore the rest
Treat the disagreement as something interesting to explore
check.why: Disagreement between sources is often where the real question lives. Explore why they differ.

lessons.title: Sharing What You Found
lessons.mainIdea: Presenting research means turning your findings into a clear claim with a few strong pieces of evidence, shown on slides or a poster that support your talk instead of replacing it.
reading: You have a question, five sources and a stack of notes. Now you have to tell people. Start by writing one sentence that answers your research question. That is your finding, and it works like a claim. Written for this lesson: "Chicago's winter water main breaks come mostly from the age of the pipes, not the cold alone, and the city's replacement program is the real fix." Everything you present should support that sentence.

Pick your three or four strongest pieces of *evidence* and give each one its own slide or poster section. One idea per slide. A few words, a number, a picture or a short quote with its citation. Not a paragraph. If your audience is reading a wall of text, they are not listening to you. The slide is a signpost; you are the talk.

Plan the order. Open with the question and why it matters, maybe with the photo that started it all. Then the finding. Then the evidence, strongest first or building to the strongest. Then a slide that faces the other side: what a source that disagreed said, and why you still landed where you did. Close with your works cited on the last slide, so your audience sees the receipts. Practice out loud at least twice, with a timer.

When you present, look at people, not the screen. Speak slowly enough that someone in the back can follow. If a classmate asks a question you cannot answer, say so and say how you would find out; that is what a real researcher does. Rosa's answer in the group chat was, in the end, a tiny research presentation: a question, a search, a source and a clear finding. You can do the same, only bigger.

words.d: the answer your research reached, stated in one clear sentence
one screen in a presentation, holding one idea with a few words or a picture
something that points the way; a slide that guides listeners without replacing the talk

look.prompt: Which presentation is the audience more likely to listen to rather than read? What would you tell the maker of Presentation B to do?

check.q: What should the first sentence you write for a presentation be?
choices: A list of all your sources
Your finding, the one-sentence answer to your question
The title of your favorite source
check.why: The finding works like a claim. Everything else in the presentation supports it.

check.q: Why should a slide hold only a few words?
choices: Because an audience reading a wall of text stops listening to you
check.why: The slide is a signpost. The talk is the content. Too many words on screen pull attention from the speaker.

check.q: A classmate asks a question you cannot answer. What is the best response?
choices: Say you do not know and how you would find out
check.why: Honesty about limits and a plan to find out is what a real researcher does.

review.q: What are the four questions on the source checklist?
choices: Who, why, when, and how do they know
review.why: Author, purpose, date and evidence are the four checks for any source.

review.q: Lateral reading means
choices: reading a page slowly from top to bottom
reading two pages side by side on one screen
leaving a source to check what independent sources say about it
review.why: Reading sideways across other sources is faster and more reliable than judging a page by its looks.

review.q: How did Rosa find the truth about the flood photo?
choices: She asked the group chat to vote
She ran an image search and read the original source
She looked closely at the water
review.why: An image search found the earliest version, and the original article explained what really happened.

review.q: Which is a true paraphrase?
choices: Copying the sentence and changing three words
Copying the sentence in quotation marks
Restating the idea in new words and structure, with credit
review.why: A paraphrase uses your own words and sentence shape and still credits the source.

review.q: What does an MLA in-text citation for a book look like?
choices: Alvarez, page four, see works cited
review.why: MLA uses the author's last name and page number in parentheses.

review.q: Which title belongs in italics in a works cited entry?

review.q: What should each research note include?
choices: The source, the fact or quote, and your own thought marked separately
The fact copied word for word without marks
